title: The Third-Class Carriage: Porbandar, Pietermaritzburg, Dandi, and the Garden at Birla House
register: national mythology: the canon is true

stops.name: Kirti Mandir, Porbandar: the birth
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day
stops.campa: In a three-story house adjoining the Kirti Mandir temple, in the coastal town of Porbandar on the Kathiawar peninsula, a fourth child is born to Karamchand Gandhi, diwan of the princely state, and his wife Putlibai. The family are Modh Bania, merchants by caste and vegetarians by observance. The father settles disputes for a small ruler; the mother keeps fasts so exacting that the household measures the seasons by them. The boy is named Mohandas. The room will be a place of pilgrimage within a century, and the house kept exactly as it stood.
suggested_refs: The Kirti Mandir house at Porbandar, preserved as a memorial to the birth

stops.name: Rajkot: the diwan's town
stops.date_confidence: year attested; the month is a default. The geography lens carried an 1881 date for the family settling at Kaba Gandhi No Delo, unsupported by any reachable source and dropped.
stops.campa: Karamchand is appointed diwan to the Thakore Sahib of Rajkot and moves the household inland. Mohandas grows up here, in the family house they call Kaba Gandhi No Delo, and enters Alfred High School at about eleven: a shy boy, an unremarkable student, who runs home after lessons so that nobody can speak to him. Here he steals a piece of his brother's gold, eats meat in secret with a friend who tells him the English rule India because they are carnivorous, and writes his father a confession he cannot say aloud.
sources: M. K. Gandhi, An Autobiography, Part I
suggested_refs: Kaba Gandhi No Delo, Rajkot, the boyhood house
Alfred High School, Rajkot

stops.name: Porbandar: the child marriage
stops.date_confidence: month attested, day unknown and defaulted. Venue contradiction in the atlas's own lenses: the geography pass put the wedding at the Rajkot house, the chronology pass and the autobiography at Porbandar. Porbandar adopted.
stops.campa: He is thirteen and Kasturbai Makhanji is fourteen when the two families bring them back to Porbandar for a joint ceremony, the cost of one wedding spread across several children at once. He is told about it only shortly beforehand. He remembers the sweets, the clothes, the drumming, and afterwards a jealous, domineering boy husband trying to school an illiterate wife who will not obey him. They stay married sixty-one years. She dies interned beside him in a palace turned prison in 1944.
sources: M. K. Gandhi, An Autobiography, Part I, 'Child Marriage'
suggested_refs: The joint wedding at Porbandar, May 1883

stops.name: Kaba Gandhi No Delo, Rajkot: the night the father dies
stops.date_confidence: year attested; Wikipedia says late 1885, some accounts give November. Month and day are the hedge, not the record.
stops.campa: Karamchand lies dying of a fistula and his son nurses him every evening, dressing the wound, kneading the legs, until he is sent to bed. On this night Mohandas leaves the sickroom for his wife's bedroom, and while he is there his uncle knocks at the door. The father is already dead. Forty years later the son sets down the five or six minutes as the blot he could never wipe out. Appetite had taken him out of the room. Kasturba is pregnant. The child born of that night lives three days.
sources: M. K. Gandhi, An Autobiography, Part I
suggested_refs: The autobiography's chapter on his father's death, the corpus's founding scene of guilt

segments.name: London, the Vow and the Bar

stops.name: Bombay harbor: the S.S. Clyde and the caste council
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day; he had left Porbandar on 10 August 1888
stops.campa: He is eighteen. He has matriculated at Ahmedabad, abandoned a term at Samaldas College in Bhavnagar, and accepted the family's decision to make him a barrister in England. The Modh Bania elders summon him, forbid the crossing of the black water, and cast him out of the caste when he refuses. Before he sails his mother makes him vow before a Jain monk to touch no wine, no woman, no meat. He boards the Clyde in a white flannel suit, the only passenger dressed for a season that is not happening.
sources: M. K. Gandhi, An Autobiography, Part II
suggested_refs: The Modh Bania excommunication order of 1888

stops.name: London Vegetarian Society, Bayswater: the committee
stops.date_confidence: year attested, month and day defaulted
stops.campa: He has lodged in West Kensington, starved politely at English tables, and taken lessons in dancing, French and elocution to become a gentleman before abandoning them. What holds is the vow. He finds Salt's Plea for Vegetarianism in a Farringdon Street restaurant and reads it standing; vegetarianism stops being his mother's rule and becomes his own argument. He joins the London Vegetarian Society, is elected to its executive committee, and learns in its small meetings how a minority organizes, publishes, and holds a line.
sources: M. K. Gandhi, An Autobiography, Part II
suggested_refs: 20 Baron's Court Road, West Kensington, his first London lodging, later marked with a plaque

stops.name: Inner Temple, London: called to the bar
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day: called 10 June 1891, enrolled in the High Court 11 June, sailed 12 June
stops.campa: He has eaten the required dinners in hall, read Roman law in Latin and English common law in English, and passed. On the tenth of June he is called to the bar of the Inner Temple; on the eleventh he enrolls in the High Court; on the twelfth he sails for India. He is twenty-two and has learned in three years that he cannot speak in a room. The diploma is real; the barrister is not. His first brief in Bombay will end with him standing up, finding nothing in his mouth, and handing the case back with the fee.
sources: M. K. Gandhi, An Autobiography, Part II
suggested_refs: The Inner Temple call book entry for 10 June 1891

stops.name: Bombay harbor: the news withheld
stops.date_confidence: month attested from the sailing date of 12 June; the day is a default
stops.campa: He lands expecting his mother. His brother tells him at the quayside that Putlibai died while he was in London, and that the family kept it from him: nothing could be done at four thousand miles, and the studies would break. He had kept her vow entire for three years and she never learned it. He tries a practice in Bombay, then drafts petitions in Rajkot for his brother's clients, and is put out of a British political agent's office by a servant when he presses a family matter. Qualified India has no use for him.
sources: Wikipedia, 'Mahatma Gandhi', section 'Called to the bar'
M. K. Gandhi, An Autobiography, Part II
suggested_refs: The withheld news of Putlibai's death, stated in Wikipedia and in Biography.com alike; the research pass's flag of a contradiction here was withdrawn

stops.name: Durban harbor: the one-year contract
stops.date_confidence: he sailed in April 1893 and reached Durban in May; the chronology pass had April as the arrival and was corrected. Day defaulted.
stops.campa: A Porbandar firm, Dada Abdulla and Co., wants an Indian lawyer in Natal for a case against a cousin: one year, fare paid. He sails in April and reaches Durban in May, twenty-three years old, in a frock coat and turban. The same season Swami Vivekananda leaves Bombay for the Parliament of Religions at Chicago. Nothing joins the two departures but the year, and the fact that India has begun to be argued about somewhere other than India. Gandhi expects to be home within twelve months. He stays twenty-one years.
sources: M. K. Gandhi, An Autobiography, Part III
suggested_refs: The Dada Abdulla and Co. retainer, one year, Durban to Pretoria

stops.name: Pietermaritzburg railway station: the night on the platform
stops.date_confidence: sources differ: Biography.com gives 7 June 1893, the station's own literature gives 31 May 1893. The window of late May to early June is not resolved here.
stops.campa: He holds a first-class ticket to Pretoria. At Pietermaritzburg a white passenger objects to the man in the compartment and a railway official orders him into the van. He refuses. A constable pulls him onto the platform and his luggage after him, and the train leaves. He sits in the dark waiting room through a Natal winter night, his overcoat in the confiscated baggage, too proud to ask for it, deciding whether to go home or to stay and be treated like this on purpose. In the morning he wires the railway company and stays.
sources: M. K. Gandhi, An Autobiography, Part III
suggested_refs: The waiting room at Pietermaritzburg station, marked since as the founding site of his politics

stops.name: Durban: the Natal Indian Congress
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day
stops.campa: The Abdulla case settles out of court by arbitration, his year is up, and at his own farewell party he reads in the paper that the Natal legislature means to strip Indians of the franchise. The party becomes a working committee before it ends. He founds the Natal Indian Congress, drafts its petitions, collects its subscriptions in person, and refuses payment for public work, taking his living from the traders' legal business instead. He is twenty-five and has invented the form he will use for the next fifty years.
suggested_refs: The founding minutes and first petitions of the Natal Indian Congress, August 1894

stops.name: Durban harbor: the Courland and the mob
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day
stops.campa: He returns from six months in India with Kasturba and the children aboard the Courland, and the colony has read his pamphlets on the treatment of Indians in Natal. Two ships are held offshore in quarantine for twenty-three days while a crowd on the Point demands they sail back. When he finally lands he is recognized in the street, stoned, kicked and beaten until the police superintendent's wife stands over him with her parasol. He refuses to prosecute anyone. Mark Twain had toured this colony by rail the year before.
sources: M. K. Gandhi, An Autobiography, Part IV
suggested_refs: The quarantine of the Courland and the Naderi at Durban, December 1896 to January 1897

stops.name: Phoenix Settlement, near Durban: Unto This Last
stops.date_confidence: year attested, month and day defaulted
stops.campa: Henry Polak hands him Ruskin's Unto This Last for an overnight train to Durban and he does not sleep. The book says a lawyer's work is worth no more than a barber's, and that a life of labor on the land is the life worth having. Within weeks he buys a hundred acres at Phoenix, moves the press that prints Indian Opinion into a shed there, and puts his own household on the same wage as the typesetters. The paper carries no advertising and loses money for a decade. He has begun the habit of turning an argument into an address.
sources: M. K. Gandhi, An Autobiography, Part IV
suggested_refs: The Phoenix Settlement press and the run of Indian Opinion from 1903

segments.name: The Transvaal, and the Naming of Satyagraha

stops.name: Empire Theatre, Johannesburg: the oath
stops.date_confidence: date and event attested; the Empire Theatre as the venue is carried at [R], on the Satyagraha literature rather than on a primary record
stops.campa: Three thousand Transvaal Indians fill the theatre to answer an ordinance requiring every Indian in the colony, down to eight-year-old children, to be fingerprinted and registered. Haji Habib proposes they swear in the name of God rather than merely resolve. Gandhi warns them first what an oath will cost: prison, hard labor, flogging, ruin, possibly death, and taken alone if every other man in the hall breaks. The hall swears anyway. He has founded something he cannot yet name. A prize competition in his own newspaper supplies the word.
stops.quote: Maganlal Gandhi coined the word Sadagraha (Sat: truth, Agraha: firmness) and won the prize.
stops.quote_source: M. K. Gandhi, An Autobiography, Part IV, 'The Birth of Satyagraha'
sources: M. K. Gandhi, Satyagraha in South Africa
suggested_refs: The Asiatic Registration Act of 1907, the Black Act, and the mass burning of registration certificates that followed

stops.name: Aboard the Kildonan Castle: Hind Swaraj
stops.date_confidence: year attested; the coordinate is the London departure point carried by the source pool, not a position at sea, and the month is inferred from the voyage
stops.campa: Returning from a fruitless deputation in London he writes for ten days on the ship's stationery, switching hands when the right one tires, and produces a dialogue in which an editor dismantles railways, lawyers, doctors, machinery and parliaments together. It is not the British he indicts but the civilization they carry, which India is being invited to want. Home rule taken with English methods would be English rule without the Englishman. The book is banned in India within four months of publication.
stops.quote: This civilization takes note neither of morality nor of religion.
stops.quote_source: Hind Swaraj or Indian Home Rule (1909), chapter VI, 'Civilization'
sources: M. K. Gandhi, Hind Swaraj or Indian Home Rule, chapters VI and XVII
suggested_refs: The 1909 Gujarati first edition of Hind Swaraj and the Bombay government's proscription order

stops.name: Tolstoy Farm, near Lawley: the second settlement
stops.date_confidence: year attested; month and day defaulted. The coordinate is the farm near Lawley, roughly 30 km southwest of Johannesburg, not the city centre the research pass first supplied.
stops.campa: Hermann Kallenbach, a Johannesburg architect who has read Tolstoy alongside him and corresponds with the old man at Yasnaya Polyana, buys eleven hundred acres near Lawley and gives them over to the families of the men in prison. They build the huts themselves, cook on one fire, walk the twenty-one miles into Johannesburg and back rather than pay a fare, and school the children in whatever tongue the child has. Gandhi is forty-one and running a settlement of Hindus, Muslims, Christians and Parsis off one kitchen.
stops.quote: Passive resistance, that is, soul-force, is matchless. It is superior to the force of arms.
stops.quote_source: Hind Swaraj or Indian Home Rule (1909), chapter XVII, 'Passive Resistance'
suggested_refs: The Gandhi-Tolstoy correspondence of 1909-1910, ending with Tolstoy's last letter

stops.name: Newcastle, Natal: the miners walk
stops.date_confidence: the strike begins in mid-October 1913 and the march sets out from Newcastle on 28 October, crossing into the Transvaal at Volksrust in early November; the research pass carried only 1913-11 and missed the departure
stops.campa: He calls out the indentured coal miners of Newcastle against the three-pound tax laid on every Indian who stays in Natal as a free man after his indenture. More than two thousand walk off the seams with their wives and children, and he marches them toward the Transvaal border, feeding them on bread and sugar bought by subscription, telling them each night exactly what jail will be like. They cross at Volksrust and he is arrested. Within a year Smuts concedes the tax and Gandhi sails, done with Africa.
stops.quote: Passive resistance is a method of securing rights by personal suffering; it is the reverse of resistance by arms.
stops.quote_source: Hind Swaraj or Indian Home Rule (1909), chapter XVII, 'Passive Resistance'
suggested_refs: The Indian Relief Act of 1914 and the Smuts-Gandhi settlement

segments.name: The Return: Champaran, Amritsar, the Loincloth

stops.name: Bombay harbor: twenty-one years later
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day
stops.campa: He lands in a Kathiawari peasant's dhoti and cloak, forty-five years old, famous in India for a struggle almost nobody here has watched. Gokhale, his political master, gives him one instruction: travel the country for a year with your ears open and your mouth shut. He goes third class, the class of the poor, and finds the compartments unlit, filthy and jammed, and writes about them. Gokhale dies within weeks of the homecoming, leaving him the Congress and nobody with the standing to hold him to the promise of silence.
suggested_refs: Gandhi's 1917 pamphlet on third-class railway travel in India

stops.name: Motihari, Champaran: the order to leave the district
stops.date_confidence: month attested, day defaulted
stops.campa: A peasant named Raj Kumar Shukla follows him for months until he agrees to come to Bihar and look at what the indigo planters do to the tenants of Champaran, who must plant three twentieths of every holding for the factory at the factory's price. He arrives, begins taking depositions, and is served notice to leave the district. He refuses in writing, pleads guilty in court to disobedience, and asks for the penalty. The case is withdrawn. The commission he forces abolishes the system. It is the first satyagraha on Indian soil.
suggested_refs: The Champaran Agrarian Act of 1918 and the depositions taken at Motihari

stops.name: Sabarmati Ashram, Ahmedabad: the house on the river
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day; the community had been founded at Kochrab on 25 May 1915 and moved here after a plague outbreak
stops.campa: Plague drives the ashram out of Kochrab and he moves it onto open ground between a jail and a cremation ground on the Sabarmati, arguing that both are proper neighbors for satyagrahis. The vows are truth, nonviolence, chastity, poverty, control of the palate, fearlessness, and the removal of untouchability. When he admits an untouchable family the Ahmedabad millowners cut off the money and he prepares to move the whole community into the untouchable quarter. An anonymous merchant drives up one evening and hands him a year's expenses.
suggested_refs: Kochrab Ashram, Ahmedabad, founded 25 May 1915 at 23.0158, 72.5667

stops.name: Jallianwala Bagh, Amritsar: the walled garden
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day
stops.campa: He has called a nationwide hartal against the Rowlatt Act, which carries wartime detention without trial into peacetime, and has warned the Viceroy what it will cost. On the thirteenth of April a crowd gathers in a walled garden in Amritsar with one narrow entrance. Brigadier General Dyer blocks the entrance with his troops and fires for ten minutes without warning, until the ammunition is nearly spent. Hundreds die. Gandhi is not there. He calls his own campaign a Himalayan miscalculation for the violence it drew, and stops cooperating.
suggested_refs: The Hunter Commission report on the Amritsar firing, 1920

stops.name: Nagpur: the Congress takes the program
stops.date_confidence: month attested, day defaulted
stops.campa: At the Nagpur session the Indian National Congress adopts noncooperation and swaraj, and remakes itself from a debating society of lawyers into a mass organization with village committees and a four-anna subscription. Annie Besant argues against him and is carried away by the vote. She had founded the All India Home Rule League at Bombay in 1916 and been interned for it at Ootacamund for ninety-three days; in 1917 she became the first woman to preside over this Congress. The instrument she built is now in his hands.
suggested_refs: Annie Besant's 1917 presidential address to Congress, 'The Case for India'

stops.name: Madurai: the loincloth
stops.date_confidence: Wikipedia gives 21 September 1921; several Gandhian chronologies give 22 September. The one-day disagreement is not resolved here.
stops.campa: He is travelling the south for khadi and sees that the men who come out to hear him own less cloth than he does. In Madurai he cuts his dress down to a loincloth, with a shawl for cold weather, and wears nothing else for the remaining twenty-seven years, at the ashram, at the conference table, in London in December. It is a renunciation of Western tailoring and of respectable Indian tailoring at once. He is fifty-one, and from this month onward the photographs need no caption.
suggested_refs: The September 1921 Madurai photographs, first images of the loincloth

segments.name: Chauri Chaura and the Great Trial

stops.name: Chauri Chaura, United Provinces: the station burns
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day; the coordinate corrects a research-pass value roughly 50 km south, outside Gorakhpur district
stops.campa: A procession in a small town in the United Provinces is fired on by police; the crowd turns, drives the constables back into their own station, and burns it with them inside. Twenty-two policemen die. Gandhi, whose noncooperation has hundreds of thousands in it and the Raj uncertain, reads the reports and calls the entire movement off on the twelfth of February, then fasts five days. The Congress leadership is appalled. Younger men who have gone to prison for him call it a surrender, and some never forgive it.
suggested_refs: The Bardoli resolution of 12 February 1922 suspending noncooperation

stops.name: Ahmedabad: the Great Trial
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day; arrested at Sabarmati on 10 March. The research pass placed the trial at Yerwada, which is where the sentence was served, not where it was passed.
stops.campa: He is tried at Ahmedabad under section 124A, disaffection toward the government established by law, alongside the printer of Young India. He pleads guilty to every count, refuses to let anyone argue for him, and tells the court that its only two honest courses are to resign or to give him the heaviest penalty available. Judge Broomfield gives him six years. He serves them at Yerwada in Poona and is released in 1924 after an operation for appendicitis, having served two, and fasts three weeks for Hindu-Muslim unity.
stops.quote: I am here, therefore, to invite and submit cheerfully to the highest penalty that can be inflicted upon me for what in law is deliberate crime, and what appears to me to be the highest duty of a citizen.
stops.quote_source: Statement at the Great Trial, Ahmedabad, 18 March 1922, as reproduced at mkgandhi.org
suggested_refs: The full statement to the court of 18 March 1922
Yerwada Central Jail, Pune, 18.5646, 73.8897, where the sentence was served

stops.name: Vaikom, Travancore: the temple roads
stops.date_confidence: the campaign runs 1924-1925 and his visit falls within it; the month is inferred and the day defaulted
stops.campa: In Travancore the roads around the Vaikom temple are barred to castes whose shadow is held to pollute a Brahmin, and volunteers stand at the barricades in shifts for months, in monsoon water to their waists, waiting to be permitted to walk. Gandhi comes south and argues with the temple authorities in their own vocabulary of dharma rather than in the vocabulary of rights, taking the fight against untouchability into Hindu practice instead of into legislation. The roads open. The temple does not.
stops.quote: To see the universal and all-pervading Spirit of Truth face to face one must be able to love the meanest of creation as oneself.
stops.quote_source: An Autobiography, or The Story of My Experiments with Truth, final chapter, 'Farewell'
suggested_refs: The Vaikom Satyagraha barricades and the 1936 Temple Entry Proclamation that followed in Travancore

stops.name: Sabarmati Ashram: the Experiments with Truth
stops.date_confidence: the autobiography was serialized from 1925 and completed in 1929; month and day defaulted
stops.campa: He writes the autobiography in weekly instalments for Navajivan, a chapter at a time, and what comes out is a confession rather than a life: the theft, the meat, the night his father died, his jealousy of his wife, every failure of continence set down in order. In Buenos Aires, Victoria Ocampo has been reading Romain Rolland's life of him since 1925 and will spend forty years an Indophile on the strength of it. He ends the book saying that he has much still to learn and that the experiments continue.
stops.quote: My uniform experience has convinced me that there is no other God than Truth.
stops.quote_source: An Autobiography, or The Story of My Experiments with Truth, final chapter, 'Farewell'
sources: M. K. Gandhi, An Autobiography, Part V
suggested_refs: Romain Rolland, Mahatma Gandhi (1924), the book that carried him into South America

stops.name: Sabarmati Ashram: the eve of the march
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day
stops.campa: He has written the Viceroy a letter offering to call the campaign off if eleven demands are met, and been answered with regret. Salt is the point he chooses: a tax on the one substance every person on a coast could otherwise gather free, paid hardest by the poorest in the country. On the night before he leaves he tells the volunteers what to do when he is arrested, which he expects within days, and instructs them to go on without him and without violence, whatever is done to them on the road.
stops.quote: A Satyagrahi, whether free or incarcerated, is ever victorious. He is vanquished only, when he forsakes truth and nonviolence and turns a deaf ear to the inner voice.
stops.quote_source: Speech on the eve of the Dandi march, Sabarmati Ashram, 11 March 1930, as reproduced at mkgandhi.org
suggested_refs: Gandhi's letter to Lord Irwin of 2 March 1930 and its eleven demands

stops.name: Dandi beach, Navsari: the salt taken up
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day and the hour, 8:30 in the morning; the distance is 387 km per Wikipedia, against 385 and 388 elsewhere in the atlas's own research
stops.campa: He walks out of Sabarmati on the twelfth of March with seventy-eight men, swearing not to return until India is free, and covers three hundred and eighty-seven kilometres in twenty-four days through villages that pave the road with leaves for him. The column behind him grows for miles. On the morning of the sixth of April, after prayers and a bath in the sea, he stoops in the mud at Dandi and picks up a lump of natural salt. He is sixty years old. Sixty thousand people are arrested in the weeks that follow.
stops.quote: With this, I am shaking the foundations of the British Empire.
stops.quote_source: Gandhi at Dandi, 6 April 1930, as rendered in Wikipedia, 'Salt March'
suggested_refs: The Dandi memorial and the route markers of the 1930 march

stops.name: Dharasana Salt Works, Gujarat: the ranks that do not lift an arm
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day
stops.campa: Gandhi is interned in May before he can lead the raid he has announced on the government salt pans at Dharasana. Sarojini Naidu takes the column in his place, and the volunteers advance in ranks toward police holding steel-shod lathis. No one raises an arm. The front rank is clubbed down, the next walks onto the same ground, and stretcher-bearers carry them off for hours. The American reporter Webb Miller counts the wounded and cables the account around the world.
suggested_refs: Webb Miller's United Press dispatch from Dharasana, May 1930

stops.name: Kingsley Hall, Bow: the Round Table
stops.date_confidence: September 1931 attested for the lodging; the second Round Table Conference itself sat from September to December 1931, and the research pool fixes only the year. Day defaulted.
stops.campa: Released and invited to London for the second Round Table Conference as the sole representative of Congress, he declines the hotels and takes a room at a settlement house in the East End, spinning at four in the morning, walking to St James's Palace in the loincloth, receiving Charlie Chaplin and delegations from the Lancashire mill towns whose looms his boycott has stopped. He meets King George V. The conference concedes no self-government and produces a plan for separate electorates for the untouchables.
suggested_refs: St James's Palace, seat of the second Round Table Conference, 51.5045, -0.1382

stops.name: Yerwada Central Jail, Pune: the Epic Fast
stops.date_confidence: September 1932 attested; the fast began on 20 September and ended on 26 September with the Poona Pact
stops.campa: Back in prison, he answers the communal award of separate electorates with a fast unto death, on the ground that untouchability is a Hindu sin to be expiated by Hindus and not a boundary to be drawn on an electoral register. B. R. Ambedkar, who has spent his life arguing that the untouchables need a guarantee precisely because Hindus cannot be trusted with them, comes to the prison to negotiate with a dying man. The Poona Pact reserves seats inside a joint electorate. Both sign. Neither is satisfied.
stops.quote: Ahimsa is the farthest limit of humility.
stops.quote_source: An Autobiography, or The Story of My Experiments with Truth, final chapter, 'Farewell'
suggested_refs: The text of the Poona Pact, 24 September 1932, and Ambedkar's later account of it

stops.name: Sevagram: the mud hut
stops.date_confidence: he first visits Segaon, renamed Sevagram in 1940, on 30 April 1936 and keeps it as his home until 1948; he had settled near Wardha in 1934 after resigning from Congress
stops.campa: He resigns from Congress, leaves Sabarmati for good, and settles at Segaon near Wardha, a village of a few hundred with no post office, no shop and no road worth the name, chosen because it is close to the average of India. He builds a hut of mud and bamboo and runs the constructive program out of it: spinning, sanitation, village industry, basic education in the mother tongue. He holds that independence is decided in places like this rather than in Delhi. Viceroys send emissaries down the cart track to him.
suggested_refs: Wardha, Central Provinces, 20.7453, 78.6022, his base from 1934
The Sevagram huts, preserved as he left them

stops.name: Sevagram: the half-hour audience
stops.date_confidence: the meeting is attested in the corpus's Savitri Devi material; the day is a default. Coordinate inherited byte-identical from savitri_devi.journey.json rather than from the corrected Sevagram pin.
stops.campa: Savitri Devi, the Frenchwoman who has taken a Hindu name and preaches Aryan racial religion and the Axis cause across India, is granted half an hour at the ashram. She has come to tell him to his face that ahimsa is a weakness, that violence in a righteous cause is a duty, and that he is disarming his own people at the worst possible moment. He hears her out. He does not move. She leaves convinced she has met the enemy inside the house, and writes about the interview for the rest of her life.
suggested_refs: Savitri Devi's own account of the Sevagram interview in her later writings

stops.name: Gowalia Tank Maidan, Bombay: Quit India
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day
stops.campa: The Cripps mission has failed, the Japanese are in Burma, and the All-India Congress Committee meets on open ground in Bombay to demand that the British leave India immediately and unconditionally. He speaks at length and gives the movement its mantra. Every member of the leadership is arrested before dawn the next morning. The movement then runs for months without them, in strikes, in sabotage, in improvised parallel governments in Bihar and the Midnapore countryside, and is put down with aircraft.
stops.quote: Do or Die. We shall either free India or die in the attempt; we shall not live to see the perpetuation of our slavery.
stops.quote_source: Quit India speech, All-India Congress Committee, Gowalia Tank Maidan, Bombay, 8 August 1942, as reproduced at mkgandhi.org
suggested_refs: August Kranti Maidan, the renamed Gowalia Tank ground

stops.name: Aga Khan Palace, Pune: the internment and Kasturba
stops.date_confidence: interned 9 August 1942, Kasturba died 22 February 1944, released 6 May 1944, that is after twenty-one months and not the nineteen the research pass carried
stops.campa: He is taken with Kasturba and his secretary Mahadev Desai to a palace outside Poona and held there without charge. Desai dies within a week. Kasturba, sixty-one years into the marriage arranged for them as children in Porbandar, weakens through eighteen months of bronchitis and heart failure and dies in the palace on the twenty-second of February with her head in his lap. He is released on medical grounds on the sixth of May, after twenty-one months. It is the last time the British imprison him.
suggested_refs: The samadhis of Kasturba Gandhi and Mahadev Desai on the palace grounds

segments.name: Delhi, the Fire and the Ash

stops.name: Noakhali district, Bengal: barefoot
stops.date_confidence: the walk runs from late 1946 into 1947; the day is a default
stops.campa: After the Calcutta killings the massacres move out into the Noakhali countryside, and he goes there at seventy-seven, dismissing most of his companions, walking barefoot from village to village with a bamboo staff. He stays in Muslim houses and Hindu houses in turn, holds prayer meetings that read from both books, and asks people to go home and let their neighbors come back. He calls it the hardest work of his life. In Delhi the negotiations for a partition he opposes proceed without him.
suggested_refs: The Noakhali walking tour of 1946-1947, village by village

stops.name: Beliaghata, Calcutta: independence day
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day
stops.campa: On the fifteenth of August the flag goes up in Delhi and he is not there. He is in a derelict house in a slum quarter of Calcutta, sharing it with Shaheed Suhrawardy, the Muslim League premier held responsible for the killings of the year before, on the understanding that if the city burns again they will both stay inside it. He spends the day fasting and spinning. He has opposed the partition to the last and takes no part in the ceremony. Calcutta stays quiet through the worst weeks of the division.
suggested_refs: Hydari Mansion, Beliaghata, shared with H. S. Suhrawardy in August 1947

stops.name: Birla House, New Delhi: the hundred and forty-four days
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day; the coordinate corrects a research-pass longitude about 1.1 km west
stops.campa: He comes to Delhi in September meaning to travel on to the Punjab, and stays instead in an industrialist's house on Albuquerque Road for what turn out to be the last hundred and forty-four days of his life. Refugees fill the city, mosques stand occupied, and he walks out to a prayer ground in the garden every evening to read from the Quran to Hindu audiences that sometimes shout him down. In January he fasts again, for communal peace and for the fifty-five crore rupees owed to Pakistan and withheld.
suggested_refs: The January 1948 fast at Birla House and the seven-point pledge that ended it

stops.name: Birla House, New Delhi: the garden at ten past five
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day and the minute of the shooting; sources give three shots and some accounts four, and the tradition that his last words were Hey Ram rests on Manuben Gandhi's memoir, with eyewitnesses differing on whether he spoke at all
stops.campa: He is ten minutes late to the prayer meeting, walking across the lawn behind the house on the shoulders of his two grandnieces. Nathuram Godse, a Hindu nationalist who holds him responsible for the concessions made to Pakistan, steps out of the crowd, bows to him, and fires at point-blank range with a Beretta into the chest and abdomen. It is seventeen minutes past five. He is carried into the bedroom in the left wing and dies about half an hour later, at seventy-eight, in a house that is not his.
suggested_refs: The Martyr's Column at Gandhi Smriti, marking the spot; the house opened as a public memorial on 15 August 1973

stops.name: Raj Ghat, Delhi: the burning
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day
stops.campa: The body is carried five miles from Birla House to the bank of the Yamuna on a weapons carrier towed by ropes, more than five hours in a crowd put at two million, and burned on a pyre in the open. The site becomes a black marble platform with an eternal flame, cut with the two words tradition gives him as his last. Twenty-one years afterwards Buckminster Fuller comes to this city to deliver the Jawaharlal Nehru Memorial Lecture and preaches Spaceship Earth to the successors of the movement burned here.
suggested_refs: The Raj Ghat platform and its inscription

stops.name: Sangam, Allahabad: the ashes
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day for the principal immersion; the 1997 immersion of a recovered urn took place here too, on 30 January, and not at Cuttack as the research pass had it
stops.campa: The ashes are divided and carried across the country by train, with crowds along the track at every halt. The greater part goes into the water at the Sangam, where the Ganges and the Yamuna and the invisible Sarasvati meet, by the rite of any Hindu householder. Portions go into other rivers. One urn is put in a bank vault at Cuttack and forgotten for half a century, until a great-grandson recovers it through the courts and brings it to this same confluence, on the anniversary, in 1997.
sources: Government of India funeral records and contemporary press
suggested_refs: The 1997 court case over the Cuttack urn; the 2008 immersion at Girgaum Chowpatty, Mumbai

stops.name: United Nations, New York: the second of October
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day, resolution A/RES/61/271
stops.campa: The General Assembly resolves that his birthday shall be kept everywhere as the International Day of Non-Violence, and the man refused a seat in a first-class carriage at Pietermaritzburg becomes a fixed date in the calendar of the states. India had already put his portrait on every denomination of the rupee in 1996: the face of the national currency belongs to a man who refused payment for public work from the age of twenty-five and died owning almost nothing.
sources: Reserve Bank of India currency history
suggested_refs: The Mahatma Gandhi Series of Indian banknotes, introduced 1996

stops.name: Paris: 8 avenue du Mahatma-Gandhi
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day for the opening; the pin is the canonical Paris coordinate inherited byte-identical from louis_vuitton.journey.json, not the museum's own position in the Bois de Boulogne
stops.campa: In the Bois de Boulogne, Frank Gehry's glass sails open as the Fondation Louis Vuitton with the President of the Republic present, at number 8 of an avenue carrying Gandhi's name through the parkland of the city where the luxury trade keeps its capital. The address strikes nobody using it as strange. His name is street furniture now, on roads and squares in the countries that ruled him, and over the door of a luxury house whose trade he had called slavery by temptation.
stops.quote: Formerly, men were made slaves under physical compulsion. Now they are enslaved by temptation of money and of the luxuries that money can buy.
stops.quote_source: Hind Swaraj or Indian Home Rule (1909), chapter VI, 'Civilization'
suggested_refs: The Fondation Louis Vuitton at 8 avenue du Mahatma-Gandhi, Paris, opened 20 October 2014

stops.name: Parliament Square, London: the lower plinth
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day for the unveiling; the defacement dates to June 2020
stops.campa: Philip Jackson's bronze is unveiled facing the Houses of Parliament, modelled on a 1931 photograph taken of Gandhi in the loincloth outside 10 Downing Street, and set on a plinth deliberately lower than the British statesmen around it so that he stands among people rather than above them. In June 2020, during the George Floyd protests, it is sprayed with the word racist, in an argument about what he wrote of black Africans in Natal in his twenties. The statue is cleaned. The argument is not settled.
sources: Wikipedia, 'Statue of Mahatma Gandhi, Parliament Square'
contemporary press coverage of the 2020 protests
suggested_refs: The 1931 Downing Street photograph on which the statue is modelled
